subject: general
question: Which of the following statements is correct regarding action and reaction forces?

options.text: The action and reaction forces act on the same body and cancel each other out.
Action and reaction forces are equal, opposite and act on different bodies.
The action is always greater in magnitude than the reaction.
The internal action and reaction forces between different parts of a system do not cancel out.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Action and reaction forces are equal, opposite and act on different bodies.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The principle of action and reaction forces is based on **Newton's Third Law of Motion**, which states that "For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction."
 
• The action and reaction forces act on **different objects**, not on the same object, which is why they do not cancel each other out.
 
• The forces are **equal in magnitude** and **opposite in direction**.
 
• For example, when a person pushes against a wall, the wall exerts an equal and opposite force back on the person.
 
• These forces are fundamental to understanding interactions in mechanics, such as propulsion, collisions, and equilibrium.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **First Law (Law of Inertia)**

 
 
• What it says: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion (constant velocity in a straight line) unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force.
 
• Concept: This introduces inertia, the tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion, with mass being the measure of inertia.
 
• Example: A soccer ball on the field stays put until kicked; once rolling, it keeps going until friction or a player stops it.
 
 
 
• **Second Law (F=ma)**
 
 
• What it says: The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force applied to it and inversely proportional to its mass (Force = mass × acceleration).
